title: Heme & Endo Exam 2 Hub
examInfo: Exam 2: 50 multiple-choice questions. 45 are on the new material, lectures 11-16 (8 on L11, 9 on L12, 7 each on L13, L14, L15 and L16), and 5 are on Exam 1 material from L2, L3, L6 and L10.

L16 is the last lecture on Exam 2, so L17 Pregnancy and lactation and L18 Estrogens and androgens aren't on it. Neither is Dr. Taylor's Lecture A (Dental endocrinology): Dr. Herr says he left it off, so it will likely be on Exam 3. This hub leaves all three out.
Friday, November 13, 10:00-11:30 am (the dental students' sitting; optometry sits at 8:00).
In person, Volker Hall Lecture Room B, on Canvas with LockDown Browser, as for Exam 1.
L11 Diabetes pharmacology, L12 Endocrine pathology (both hours), L13-L14 Male and female reproductive histology, L15-L16 Male and female reproductive physiology.

Wednesday, November 11, 2:00-2:50 pm, with Dr. Madison. Its 20 PollEv questions are in the Question Bank as given ("Exam 2 in-class review"), each with a twin whose answer is a different choice ("Like an Exam 2 review question"), and each lecture's High Likelihood questions include them.

Two questions use a picture: the Sertoli cell (L13) and Dr. Herr's picture of the five follicle stages (L14). The hub has a numbered drawing of each, laid out like his, under its lecture's notes, with a key and picture questions in the Question Bank.

Five questions come from Exam 1, and only from L2 Hypothalamus and Pituitary, L3 Endocrinology of Growth, L6 Adrenal Gland and L10 Calcium and Phosphate Regulation: two from L2, one on which hormones work synergistically, one on how PTH maintains blood calcium, and one more. The Exam 1 Refresher (R) tags those four lectures' High Likelihood questions (Exam 1's predicted topics for them, plus the synergy and PTH questions), and the mock's five Exam 1 questions follow the same split, drawn at random from them. The Question Bank leaves R out until you tick it under Lectures, or tap "Exam 1 High likelihood" under Only.
Quiz 3 is due Thursday, November 12, at 11:59 pm. This hub uses nothing from the quizzes or the take-home.

likelyTopics.t: Exam 2 in-class review (11/11): pioglitazone and PPAR-gamma, lispro for meals, metformin on the liver, DPP-4 and the incretins, a macrovascular complication; and their twins
Choosing an insulin: rapid or regular for a meal, long-acting as basal, and the onset, peak and duration of each preparation
Which drugs cause hypoglycemia (insulin and the secretagogues) and which rarely do
Weight effects: gain with insulin, sulfonylureas, meglitinides and TZDs; loss with GLP-1 agonists; a GLP-1 agonist first for a patient with a weight problem
Metformin: first-line, mechanism, no effect at normal glucose, GI upset, B12, lactic acidosis, eGFR below 30

Situational choice with heart failure, heart disease or kidney disease: avoid TZDs (edema, macular edema), consider an SGLT2 inhibitor or semaglutide, sitagliptin the DPP-4 exception, linagliptin without renal adjustment
SGLT2 inhibitors: glucosuria, genital yeast infections, UTIs, hypotension, boxed warning for amputation
GLP-1 agonists and DPP-4 inhibitors: incretin actions, exendin-4, boxed warning for thyroid tumors, delayed gastric emptying
Secretagogues: the K-ATP channel mechanism, the need for working beta cells (C-peptide), low durability, sulfonylurea warnings
Hypoglycemia in the dental chair: fast sugar by mouth if awake, glucagon in an emergency
Diagnosis and physiology: A1C and glucose cutoffs, prediabetes, GLUT4, complications
Exam 2 in-class review (11/11): the most common functioning pituitary adenoma is the prolactinoma; and its twin
Primary vs secondary lab patterns (TSH vs free T4; the same rule for ACTH)
Papillary carcinoma histology: pale grooved nuclei, pseudoinclusions, papillae, psammoma bodies
Papillary vs follicular carcinoma: BRAF/lymphatics/multifocal/total thyroidectomy vs RAS/blood/invasion/hemithyroidectomy
Graves vs Hashimoto: stimulating vs blocking TSH-receptor antibodies, histology, epidemiology
Diabetes insipidus (central vs nephrogenic) vs SIADH (small cell lung carcinoma)
Pituitary adenomas: micro vs macro, mass effect, bitemporal hemianopsia, the functioning types
Medullary carcinoma: C cells, RET and MEN 2, amyloid, calcitonin/chromogranin/CEA, sporadic vs familial
Hypopituitarism: the 75 percent rule, Sheehan syndrome, null cell adenoma, empty sella, and its symptoms
Hypothyroid and hyperthyroid features: myxedema and cretinism (enlarged tongue), causes of hyperthyroidism
Thyroid development, follicular adenoma and anaplastic carcinoma
Exam 2 in-class review (11/11): the labs of primary hyperparathyroidism, and what excess cortisol does to glucose; and their twins
Hypoparathyroidism: causes, low calcium with high phosphate, Chvostek and Trousseau, dental root hypoplasia
Cushing syndrome lab logic: cortisol read with ACTH (pituitary, ectopic, adrenal)
Conn syndrome (renin low) versus secondary hyperaldosteronism (renin high)
Primary hyperparathyroidism: adenoma versus hyperplasia versus carcinoma, and how they are told apart
Adrenal cortex zones: salt, sugar, sex
Pseudohypoparathyroidism: end-organ resistance with high PTH
Secondary hyperparathyroidism: renal failure, all glands, fix the cause
Congenital adrenal hyperplasia: 21-hydroxylase versus 17-hydroxylase, treated with glucocorticoids
Addison disease: features, high ACTH, autoimmune cause
Pheochromocytoma (rule of 10s, Zellballen) and neuroblastoma

His labeled Sertoli cell drawing (he said it is on the exam): basal lamina, type A and type B spermatogonia, the junctional complex, primary spermatocyte, early and late spermatids, basal vs adluminal compartment

likelyTopics.t: Exam 2 in-class review (11/11): Leydig cells sit between the tubules, tight junctions make the blood-testis barrier, spermiogenesis; and their twins
Sertoli cells: shape, the blood-testis barrier and its two compartments, and their jobs (support and nourishment, ABP, AMH, inhibin, phagocytosis, no division, resistant to heat and radiation)
LH vs FSH: Leydig cells and testosterone (from the embryo through adult life) vs Sertoli cells, ABP and inhibin, and the two feedback brakes
Spermatogenesis: the terms, the three spermatogonia, meiosis and the 74 days
Inside or outside the tubule: tunica albuginea and lobules, Leydig cells between the tubules, myoid cells in the wall; lower temperature in the scrotum
Spermiogenesis: its phases, the nucleus becoming the head, Golgi to acrosome, mitochondria to the middle piece; then spermiation
The spermatic cord: the ductus deferens with the testicular artery and the pampiniform plexus (the only two other parts he said to know)

Accessory glands: seminal vesicles (70 percent, fructose, lipochrome), the prostate around the urethra (trouble urinating, PSA, alkaline first portion), bulbourethral glands (lubrication, skeletal muscle under somatic control)
The penis: two corpora cavernosa fill, the corpus spongiosum keeps the urethra open; erection by relaxed smooth muscle; point and shoot
The epididymis: its lining, its three jobs, sperm maturation and glycerophosphocholine against capacitation
The ducts in order and their linings: tubuli recti, rete testis, efferent ductules (cilia) vs ductus deferens, epididymis and vas (stereocilia)
Identifying the five follicle stages, and the Graafian follicle's wall from the antrum out
likelyTopics.basis: image on the exam + focus list + recording

likelyTopics.t: Exam 2 in-class review (11/11): the corona radiata and the peg cells of the uterine tube; their twins, and the granulosa cells' gap junctions
Granulosa versus theca: junctions, the zona pellucida, liquor folliculi, LH and FSH
FSH grows 10 to 12 antral follicles, LH matures and ovulates the dominant one; primordial to Graafian takes many months
Uterine tube: ciliated and peg cells, folds in all regions, poorly defined muscularis, capacitation

The uterine wall: endometrium (simple columnar epithelium, simple branched glands, functionalis with helical arteries and basalis), myometrium (inner longitudinal, middle circular with the stratum vasculare, outer longitudinal), perimetrium

The endometrium during menstruation: the functionalis (spiral arteries, follows estrogen and progesterone, shed) vs the basalis (straight arteries, untouched, regrows it); progesterone drops, the spiral arteries constrict, ischemia, shedding
The two meiotic arrests: prophase I until the LH surge, metaphase II until fertilization
His cycle graph by day: follicles, ovulation on days 13 to 15, FSH and LH peaks, estrogen and progesterone, and the uterine phases
Ovulation: the LH surge, rupture into the peritoneum, and the corpus luteum's lutein cells and fate
The linings of the cervix and vagina (the transformation zone, glycogen and lactobacilli) and the cervical plug
Milk production (prolactin) versus ejection (oxytocin), and colostrum
Oocyte numbers from the fetus to menopause
Pregnancy and the tract: corpus luteum kept, myometrium grows, cervical plug
Exam 2 in-class review (11/11): FSH acts on Sertoli cells, androgen-binding protein holds testosterone high, emission is sympathetic; and their twins
Sertoli versus Leydig cells: where each sits, FSH versus LH, what each makes (ABP, inhibin, aromatase, AMH versus testosterone) and the blood-testis barrier
Feedback: testosterone on GnRH (hypothalamus) and LH (pituitary), inhibin on FSH at the pituitary only; reading testosterone, LH and FSH patterns
Aromatase: mostly in the Sertoli cells from fetal life on (his correction of the slide), turned up by FSH; testosterone to estradiol, androstenedione to estrone; what estradiol does in men
Building a male: AMH removes the Müllerian ducts, testosterone builds the Wolffian structures (epididymis, vas deferens, seminal vesicles), DHT the penis and scrotum
Androgen insensitivity versus 5-alpha-reductase deficiency: what forms, what puberty brings, how each presents
Point and shoot: erection and lubrication parasympathetic, emission and ejaculation sympathetic
Erection and sildenafil: NO dilates the cavernosal arteries, guanylate cyclase and cGMP, compressed veins, PDE5 blocked
Spermatogenesis and the sperm: the cell sequence, four haploid spermatids, the acrosome and midpiece, maturation in the epididymis
Making testosterone: Leydig cells, LH, cholesterol desmolase (rate-limiting), adrenal androgens; testosterone across life

The accessory glands: seminal vesicles 60 to 70 percent (fructose, prostaglandins, the fibrinogen clot), prostate 20 to 30 percent (PSA breaks the clot), Cowper's lubrication; temperature, 34 degrees Celsius
Exam 2 in-class review (11/11): progesterone rules the luteal phase, FSH raises aromatase, high estradiol sets off the LH surge; and their twins

Follicular versus luteal phase, compared: proliferative, estrogen, the follicle, fertilization; secretory, progesterone, the corpus luteum, implantation, a slight rise in temperature (day 10 estradiol, day 21 progesterone)
Two cells, two gonadotropins: FSH, granulosa, aromatase, estradiol; LH, theca, cholesterol desmolase (P450scc, the rate-limiting step), testosterone; theca like Leydig, granulosa like Sertoli
Feedback: progesterone negative only; estradiol negative, then positive above 200 pg/mL for the LH surge; inhibin keeps FSH's peak small
Ovulation: LH receptors on the preovulatory follicle, collagenase and prostaglandins, OMI falls and meiosis I resumes, 14 days before menses
Estrogen and progesterone on the lining and the cervical mucus (and the myometrium, on the slide)
The three estrogens: estradiol in the reproductive years, estriol in pregnancy, estrone (adrenal DHEA) in menopause
Menopause: atresia, lost negative feedback, high GnRH, LH and FSH, estrone, hot flashes linked to GnRH
The follicle's life: granulosa cells (primary), then layers and theca cells (secondary), an antrum, one dominant follicle; the corpus luteum, its 14 days and menses
The default pathway: no AMH (Müllerian ducts form), no testosterone (Wolffian ducts regress), no DHT (female external genitalia)
Amenorrhea: primary (genetic, Turner syndrome) versus secondary (pregnancy, lactation, menopause, hyperprolactinemia; prolactin turns GnRH down)
L2 Hypothalamus and Pituitary: Exam 2 in-class review (11/11): a steroid hormone binds an intracellular receptor; and its twin, the peptide's surface receptor
L2 Hypothalamus and Pituitary: Paracrine vs neuroendocrine vs endocrine
L2 Hypothalamus and Pituitary: Receptors: Gs, Gq and Gi; insulin is a tyrosine kinase, GH uses JAK2
L2 Hypothalamus and Pituitary: Steroid vs peptide vs amine hormones: storage, transport, receptor
L2 Hypothalamus and Pituitary: Primary vs secondary from the labs
L2 Hypothalamus and Pituitary: Feedback: what feeds back, and where (short and long loops)
L2 Hypothalamus and Pituitary: The posterior pituitary only stores and releases; dopamine holds prolactin down
L10 Calcium and Phosphate Regulation: Which hormones synergize: PTH and vitamin D (calcitriol) raise blood calcium together
L10 Calcium and Phosphate Regulation: How PTH maintains blood calcium: bone, the kidney, and the gut through calcitriol; calcium up, phosphate down
L3 Endocrinology of Growth: Thyroid hormone (T3) works synergistically with GH on bone growth
L3 Endocrinology of Growth: Regulation of GH secretion: GHRH (Gs) vs somatostatin (Gi), sleep, ghrelin
L3 Endocrinology of Growth: Regulation of GH secretion: feedback by GH and IGF-1 (they raise somatostatin)
L3 Endocrinology of Growth: GH and IGF-1: linear growth runs through IGF-1 (somatomedin)
L3 Endocrinology of Growth: Major metabolic effects of GH: diabetogenic, lipolytic, builds muscle protein
L3 Endocrinology of Growth: GH excess or deficiency: gigantism vs acromegaly, short stature, a receptor defect
L3 Endocrinology of Growth: Changes in GH with aging (somatopause): from the 30s, hypothalamic
L6 Adrenal Gland: Aldosterone: keep sodium, lose potassium
L6 Adrenal Gland: Cortisol reaches the medulla and turns on PNMT
L6 Adrenal Gland: ACTH is cortisol's regulator (the HPA axis)
L6 Adrenal Gland: Cortisol raises glucose for stress
L6 Adrenal Gland: Addison's vs Cushing's; cholesterol desmolase
L10 Calcium and Phosphate Regulation: The chief cell paradox: calcium on the CaSR stops PTH
L10 Calcium and Phosphate Regulation: PTH turns on 1α-hydroxylase; calcitriol works in the gut
L10 Calcium and Phosphate Regulation: PTH in the kidney: keep calcium, dump phosphate
L10 Calcium and Phosphate Regulation: PTH acts on osteoblasts, which signal osteoclasts
L10 Calcium and Phosphate Regulation: Calcitonin on the osteoclast
L10 Calcium and Phosphate Regulation: Primary hyperparathyroidism: high PTH and calcium, low phosphate, stones

fans.text: For the record, my glucose is normal. Timmy says that's because I don't have a pancreas. I say it's the metformin. Also, I got the whole lightning round right, out loud, through the wall.
Dr. Fasinu's slide puts periodontal disease first under dental relevance, and still a whole episode without me. Also, that pie: brush after.
